notes:
Need to search first.I've written notes for all 27 verses, but they rest almost entirely on older commentaries and evangelical study sites. The research tool stopped working after a few searches, so I couldn't search further on sections 2 and 3. I found no Catholic or Orthodox reading of James 1, and nothing from bibleodyssey.org. I found no Lutheran, Wesleyan or Pentecostal sources, and nothing on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. Where the sources I did read disagree, I've marked the point **[Differs]**.

**Traditions of the sources:**
- **Reformed / Calvinist Baptist:** Gill (Calvinist Baptist, as labelled on studylight) and Spurgeon (quoted on enduringword).
- **Other older Protestant writers:** Matthew Henry, Burkitt, Ellicott/Punchard, Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary.
- **Modern evangelical:** Guzik (charismatic-leaning, on enduringword), MacArthur and Moo (both quoted on preceptaustin) and Utley (on bible.org).
- **Modern but not evangelical:** Barclay.

---

**v. 1**
- James calls himself only a servant (literally a slave). He leaves out his family tie to Jesus and doesn't claim the title "apostle." Barnes points out that other apostles also leave the title out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/james/1-1.htm
- Guzik says this humility is striking because James was Jesus' half-brother. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- Barclay says the word "slave" implies complete obedience, humility and loyalty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/james-1.html
- Gill reads "servant" as describing James's office as a preacher. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-1.html
- **Who the readers were [Differs]:**
  - Pulpit: Jews living outside Palestine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm
  - Gill: believing Jews descended from the earlier exiles, not the Christians scattered after Stephen's death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-1.html
  - Ellicott: Jewish Christians, not unbelieving Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
- Ellicott notes that the debate over which James wrote the letter bears on the dispute about the Lord's "brothers" and Mary's perpetual virginity. He identifies the author as the Lord's brother. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
- The usual Greek greeting literally means "rejoice." Paul changes it to "grace," and James uses the same greeting in Acts 15:23. https://bible.org/seriespage/james-1

**v. 2**
- There's a wordplay: "Greetings" (rejoice) in v. 1 leads into "count it all joy" in v. 2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- James says *when* trials come, not *if*. Trials are a reason for joy, not for giving up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- Gill: God tests his people's faith through hardship, as he tested Abraham. The joy comes from what trials produce, not from the trials themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/1.htm
- Barclay compares the Christian to an athlete who welcomes hard training. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/james-1.html
- A Pulpit homily contrasts this with the Stoic, who can only submit to fate, and the Epicurean, who has no answer to suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-1.html

**v. 3**
- Trials test faith; they don't create it. They show how much faith there is. Trials met with faith produce patience, but met with grumbling they can produce bitterness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- The Greek word for "patience" means active endurance, like finishing a marathon, not passive waiting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jam/Jam_1.cfm
- Pulpit: this word means patience with circumstances, while a different word (makrothumia) means patience with people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm
- Ellicott links v. 3 to Hebrews 5:14: grace grows with use. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
- Precept Austin rejects the popular idea that troubles always mean punishment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_13-4

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: "entire" means whole, like a sacrifice without blemish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
- Pulpit: patience must be given room to work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm
- **Can we reach this maturity in this life? [Differs]**
  - Gill: no. The perfection here can't be reached in this life, which is why v. 5 assumes the readers still lack wisdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-1.html
  - Precept Austin (citing a commentator): James sets this as the goal without claiming believers reach it, yet the bar should not be lowered. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_13-4
  - A Pulpit homily: moral perfection is what God aims at in all his dealings with his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-1.html
  - I couldn't find a Wesleyan "Christian perfection" reading to set beside these.

**v. 5**
- "Lacking nothing" (v. 4) and "if any lacks" (v. 5) are a deliberate wordplay. The offer of wisdom is open to anyone, but it isn't automatic: we must ask. God is not a stingy disciplinarian. https://bible.org/seriespage/james-1
- **What wisdom is meant:**
  - Ellicott: practical wisdom for living, not deep theological knowledge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
  - Gill: first, wisdom to behave rightly in trials and to see God's hand in them, as Job did; then wisdom for all of life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/1.htm
- The Greek for "generously" also suggests sincerity and singleness of heart. God doesn't shame those who keep coming to him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_15-6

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: this verse alone shows James doesn't belittle faith. He echoes Jesus at the fig tree (Matthew 21:21). "Doubting" means hovering between belief and unbelief, leaning towards unbelief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
- Pulpit: the KJV's "wavering… wave" wordplay isn't in the Greek. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm
- Gill lists what not to doubt: whether the request is right, God's power, his will and his faithfulness. Answers come in God's own time and way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-1.html
- Barclay, citing Mayor: the doubter is like a cork tossed by waves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/james-1.html

**v. 7**
- **How strong is the warning? [Differs]**
  - Burkitt: a doubter may still receive something, but has no right to expect it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wbc/james-1.html
  - Precept Austin: James isn't demanding perfect faith before God answers. He's warning against a habitually divided heart, not ordinary weakness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_17-8
  - On the other hand, the 1:5–6 page quotes a writer saying "believe that you have and you shall have." https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_15-6
- A Pulpit homily: the doubter shuts his soul to God while claiming to open it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-1.html

**v. 8**
- Gill: the double-minded man is unsettled in thought, prayer, opinion and action. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-1.html
- Precept Austin: wavering faith spills into every area of life, and the way a man prays shows in the way he lives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_17-8

**vv. 9–10**
- **What is the poor brother's "high position"? [Differs]**
  - Gill: spiritual. He is born of God, adopted and an heir. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/1.htm
  - Ellicott: possibly an outward rise in life. He encourages humble people not to fear a higher calling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
  - A Pulpit homily: the poor man is raised up as a man "in Christ," and the rich man is stripped of greatness that was never truly his. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-1.html
- **v. 10:** Gill takes "the rich" as a rich *believer*. He offers three possible senses of "low position": the low state he was raised from, being stripped by persecution, or approaching death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/1.htm
- Guzik: trials remind the rich that their comfort belongs to this life only. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/

**v. 11**
- Ellicott offers a fresher translation and stresses that the flower's beauty is literally "of its face." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
- Gill: riches are uncertain and can vanish before death. The "sun" may stand for persecution or disaster. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-1.html
- Guzik: not only does wealth fade, the rich man himself fades too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/

**v. 12**
- **Is this "trial" or "temptation"? [Differs]**
  - Precept Austin: a neutral test. The verse says to *endure* it, not *resist* it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_112
  - Guzik, following the KJV: temptation, as one kind of trial. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- **What is the "crown of life"? [Differs]**
  - MacArthur (quoted): endurance doesn't earn eternal life; it proves that faith is real. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_112
  - Another writer on the same page: the crown is recognition at Christ's judgment seat of the character a life has produced. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_112
  - Burkitt: future happiness, pictured as a crown for its excellence and as "of life" because it lasts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wbc/james-1.html
  - Barclay describes three kinds of ancient crowns: festive, royal and the victor's laurel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/james-1.html
- Precept Austin links the verse to the doctrine of "perseverance of the saints." It also quotes Moo on why rewards are a fair motive. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_112
- Matthew Henry: the reward comes by gracious promise, not as a debt owed, and endurance must flow from love for God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_001.cfm
- Love for God shows itself in obedience. https://bible.org/seriespage/james-1

**v. 13**
- God allows tests, and may send judgments (1 Kings 22). But he never lures anyone to evil. Spurgeon (quoted): "Satan tempts: God tries," and the same event can be both. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- Calvin (quoted): when Scripture speaks of God hardening hearts, it doesn't make him the author of sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- Burkitt: if God tempted people, their sins could not justly be punished. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wbc/james-1.html
- Gill: the "temptations" of vv. 2–12 (trials God sends) differ from these (enticements to sin). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/1.htm
- The Greek command is "stop saying," which may reflect an imagined objector, a debating style James often uses. https://bible.org/seriespage/james-1

**v. 14**
- Temptation only has a hold on us because of our own fallen desires. We often give Satan too much credit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- Calvin (quoted): the root of our destruction is in us. Precept Austin adds that the sin nature is not removed in believers before glory. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_113-15
- Burkitt: temptation works through our inborn corruption. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wbc/james-1.html
- Catholic translation: the Douay-Rheims renders "desire" here as "concupiscence." https://biblehub.com/catholic/james/1-15.htm

**v. 15**
- Gill traces the stages: desire is entertained and dwelt on (conception), then acted out (sin), and every sin deserves death. He cites a close Jewish parallel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/1.htm
- Precept Austin calls this a full "reproductive cycle" running from temptation to death. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_113-15
- Guzik quotes a writer who pictures lust as a harlot seducing the mind and will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: this links back to vv. 13–15. God can't be behind temptation, because only good gifts come from him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm
- Matthew Henry: "do not wander" into wrong ideas about God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_001.cfm
- MacArthur (quoted): stop blaming others, circumstances, Satan or God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_116-18

**v. 17**
- Barclay: James borrows two technical astronomy words to stress that God never changes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/james-1.html
- Gill: the sun rises, sets and casts shadows; God does none of this. Since every good gift comes from him, evil can't. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/james/1-17.html
- Precept Austin: trusting God's goodness is a defence against the enemy's suggestion that God isn't good. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_116-18

**v. 18**
- Salvation is God's gift "of his own will," not earned. Desire gives birth to death, but God's will gives birth to new life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-1/
- A Pulpit homily: the new birth is the highest of God's gifts. Its ultimate cause is simply God's good pleasure, not human merit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-1.html
- Burkitt sees four causes of the new birth here: God as author, his will as motive, the word as instrument and the "firstfruits" as purpose. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wbc/james-1.html
- The NET Bible translates "by his sovereign plan." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/b/o/bible.php?book=Jam&chapter=1&mode=text
- As firstfruits, believers belong to God for his use. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_116-18

**v. 19**
- Ropes (quoted): "quick to listen" is mainly about hearing and obeying the word of v. 18, not just everyday conversation. Precept Austin also links the anger here to quarrelling over doctrine. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_119-20
- Matthew Henry: listen to God's word rather than airing our own opinions. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_001.cfm
- Pulpit notes a textual variant, "You know this." It calls the verse James's version of "speech is silver, silence golden." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm

**v. 20**
- Gill: anger leads people into evil, not righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-1.html
- A Pulpit homily: a preacher's scolding and a hearer's resentment both hinder the word's work. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-1.html
- Precept Austin: anger short-circuits the word's sanctifying work. It frames v. 18 as justification and vv. 19ff as ongoing sanctification. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_119-20

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: the "implanted word" is the gospel. The verse echoes the parable of the sower, and the Greek word appears elsewhere only in Wisdom 12:10, meaning "inborn." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm
- Matthew Henry: "meekness" means being willing to hear our faults and be shaped by the word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_001.cfm
- Guzik: the word saves us both now and eternally. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jam/Jam_1.cfm

**v. 22**
- Fausset (quoted): "be doers" means doing it habitually, as one's regular business. MacArthur (quoted): real Christians are characteristically doers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_122-24
- Ellicott's introduction says some theologians wrongly set James against Paul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/1.htm
- Barnes: Paul speaks of justification before God, James of a believer shown to be justified before men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/james/1-1.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- Matthew Henry: the word is a mirror that shows our sins so they can be cleansed. Many are moved while hearing and forget afterwards. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_001.cfm
- Guzik: "observing" means careful study, so even Bible experts can be forgetful hearers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jam/Jam_1.cfm
- Precept Austin: the problem is an unresponsive heart, not a poor memory. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_122-24

**v. 25**
- Pulpit reads it as "the perfect law, even the law of liberty." The word for "looks" suggests stooping to peer in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/1.htm
- Ellicott: the earnest student stoops in humility to learn the Author's will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/james-1.html
- Matthew Henry: possibly an allusion to Psalm 1. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_001.cfm
- An expositor: there is outer and inner freedom, and Christian liberty includes freedom from sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/edt/james-1.html
- I found no Lutheran law-and-gospel treatment of this verse.

**v. 26**
- Gill: someone can keep up preaching, prayer and church attendance and still have a worthless religion if his tongue is unbridled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-1.html
- The verse is about self-deception, not how others see us. Utley thinks the warning is aimed at sincere but unfruitful believers, not hypocrites. https://bible.org/seriespage/james-1

**v. 27**
- Barclay: for James, the finest worship is serving the poor and keeping personally pure, not ceremony. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/james-1.html
- A Pulpit homily: true worship is active kindness, following Christ, who "went about doing good." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/james-1.html
- An expositor: true religion must give the power to stay pure in public and working life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/edt/james-1.html

---

**Not covered:** Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Wesleyan and Pentecostal readings, other scholarly notes, and prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. Good next pages to look for are Wesley's Notes, the NET Bible notes, 1517.org on James, and New Advent on concupiscence for vv. 14–15.
